title: The Social Stability Question
text:
The Social Stability Question

Louis-Vincent Gave

Gavekal Research | 5 Nov 2026

The Roman Empire grew to dominate the Mediterranean basin, then collapsed never to be seen again (at least as a unified political identity). The Persian Empire grew to dominate the broader Middle East and the Indus Valley, but once it collapsed, it was never heard from again. The Aztec Empire dominated Central America and folded like a deck chair when confronted with the disease and weapons brought by Spanish conquistadors. We could go on, but suffice to say that, in the history of rising and falling civilizations, China stands apart as a unique case of an empire that grew to dominate its region economically and culturally, collapsed into civil war, famines and foreign invasion, then, like a phoenix, picked herself up from this devastation and lifted herself out of her collapse by her own bootstraps.According to historian Angus Maddison, China accounted for almost a third of global GDP in 1820 (32.9%), only to collapse to some 4% by 1962. Today, China accounts for approximately 18% of global GDP. China’s collapse truly kicked off with the First Opium War of 1839-42 and gathered pace with the Taiping Rebellion civil war that lasted from 1850 to 1864 (the Taiping Rebellion remains the world’s second deadliest conflict after World War II; World War I comes in third). Dismemberment at the hands of Western countries followed suit, then Japanese invasion, hyperinflation, civil war, the Great Leap Forward and Cultural Revolution polished off 150 years of sheer misery. All this to say that, after such a painful history, social stability comes at a massive premium in China.
